info.text:
Due Wed Sep 2 at class time. Traveling waves, standing waves and superposition (Knight 16.1–16.3).

Sim: Wave explorer — equation-driven single traveling wave (A, λ, k, φ, f, with a Traveling-wave toggle).

name.text: Prep3-A · Wave speed from the sim

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

In the Wave explorer, set λ = 4 m and f = 2 Hz.

What wave speed does v = fλ give?

generalfeedback.text:
8 m/s.

v = fλ = (2 Hz)(4 m) = 8 m/s.

What the relation means physically: in one period the pattern advances exactly one wavelength. Two periods per second, four metres per period, so eight metres per second.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — check your two sim settings.

feedback.text: You divided instead of multiplying. In one period the wave moves forward by one whole wavelength — that should tell you which operation you want.
You divided the wrong way round. Check the units: metres per second has to come out of metres times per-second.
An extra factor of 2 has crept in — possibly from a period-versus-frequency mix-up. Re-read the two numbers you set in the sim.

name.text: Prep3-B · What moves in a traveling wave

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

Turn on the Traveling wave toggle in the Wave explorer and press Play. First follow a single crest as it moves across the screen. Then shift your attention to one fixed location: pick a vertical gridline and watch only the height of the curve where it crosses that line.

As the wave passes, the string at that fixed location…

generalfeedback.text:
It moves up and down about its rest position, repeating every period T.

A traveling wave carries a disturbance — and the energy in it — from one place to another, but the medium itself stays put. Each point of the string performs simple harmonic motion about its own rest position, perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, with the same period T as the wave. What sweeps across the screen is the shape y(x,t) = A sin(kx − ωt), not the material.

This is the core of the wave model, and the thing most often gotten backwards: the pattern travels, the medium does not.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite — watch one fixed gridline, not one crest.

answer.text: moves up and down about its rest position, repeating every period T

feedback.text: Correct — the pattern travels; the material at each point just oscillates in place.

answer.text: travels to the right, keeping pace with the crests

feedback.text: That is what the pattern does. Fix your eye on one gridline instead of following a crest — does the material at that line actually go anywhere, or does it only rise and fall in place?

answer.text: shifts to the right until the wave has gone by, then stops

feedback.text: Let the sim keep running. Fresh crests arrive at your chosen gridline again and again — does the disturbance there ever settle, and does that point drift sideways at all?

answer.text: stays flat; only the crests and troughs elsewhere are moving

feedback.text: Watch the curve's height right at your chosen gridline as first a crest and then a trough reach it. If the whole waveform is passing through that spot, its height there cannot stay fixed.

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

The sim draws y(x,t) = A sin(kx − ωt). Match each symbol to the expression the sim's read-outs confirm for it.

generalfeedback.text:
k = 2π/λ — the wave number counts radians of phase per metre.

ω = 2πf — the angular frequency counts radians of phase per second.

v = fλ — equivalently ω/k, the speed at which a given phase travels.

T = 1/f — seconds per cycle rather than cycles per second.

Two of these are about space, two about time, and v is the bridge between them. Step any one control in the sim and the linked read-outs move together.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. Sort them first: which symbols describe the wave in space and which in time? Then step the matching control in the sim and watch which read-outs follow.

incorrectfeedback.text: Use the sim's linked read-outs: step λ and see what changes with it, then step f and do the same. The pairings follow directly.

name.text: Prep3-D · One control at a time

questiontext.text:
Sim not loading? Open the Wave explorer in a new tab.

Change one control at a time in the Wave explorer and match it to what you see happen on screen.

generalfeedback.text:
Increase A: crests get taller, nothing else. Amplitude is purely vertical — it leaves λ, k and the cycle count alone.

Increase λ: each wave is longer, so fewer full waves fit across the screen.

Increase f at fixed λ: v = fλ grows, so the pattern travels faster.

Increase φ: a positive phase makes the wave reach each value sooner, sliding the whole curve to the left.

The first one is the standard trap — amplitude is easy to confuse with “how wavy” the picture looks.

partiallycorrectfeedback.text: Some rows are right. This one really has to be done in the sim — step each control on its own and watch exactly one thing change. Amplitude is the one most people get wrong.

incorrectfeedback.text: Open the sim and step one control at a time, resetting between changes. Each of these four produces a visibly different effect.

answer.text: Fewer full waves fit on screen
More full waves fit on screen
